title: Ep 284: Relativity CEO Phil Saunders on the Future of Legal Data, Gen AI, and the Shifting Landscape of Law
author: Phil Saunders

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence
st.an: The source contains only closing remarks and provides no substantive claims, evidence or argument bearing on the cluster’s proposition about pragmatic AI adoption, experimentation or unproven transformation forecasts.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Saunders accepts the cluster’s core view that AI will transform legal workflows rather than merely accelerate isolated tasks, while humans remain critical. He materially extends it with a concrete platform-usage snapshot showing substantial non-litigation use and a capability-expansion agenda for firms and legal teams, though he does not address pricing or apprenticeship in depth.
qs: Roughly 47% of all matters and projects inside RelativityOne, which is flagged by the customer, was non-litigation.

st.t: Vendor strategy: Faster building cannot eliminate integration
st.an: Saunders accepts the broader proposition that generative AI is reshaping vendor strategy and materially extends it by describing increased R&D capacity, data-governance principles and agentic workflow augmentation. However, he does not directly address faster development, build-versus-buy decisions or the persistence of integration and adoption constraints.
qs: But to the board's credit and their support, we invested a lot more in R&D and created incremental and expansive teams in this area and hired a bunch of scientists and so on and increased our patent work, notably.
It was literally, before it was cool to say, an agentic AI workflow, literally leveraging the perception and cognition capabilities of AI.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Saunders accepts the cluster’s human-led, workflow-redesign proposition and adds concrete deployment practices: augmentative and agentic workflows, structured multi-model testing, security-first governance, cloud infrastructure and hands-on user education. His evidence is largely vendor-specific and some benefit claims remain predictive, but his operating-model detail materially develops the cluster’s selective-deployment thesis.
qs: And making real decisions like, are we here to really augment what people do today, meaning transform their work?

I could speak for Relativity that we're running 30 different models across multiple platforms and products to make sure that we understand through really a structured set of data set and a bunch of workloads to determine what is going to really drive the right outcomes in terms of performance and accuracy, cost, by the way, does matter, and reduction, if not elimination, of hallucinations and challenges.

st.t: Adoption leadership: Trust must follow customer outcomes
st.an: Saunders aligns with the cluster’s conditional optimism by presenting platform architecture and generative AI as a promising response to emerging legal-data needs. His statement is a strategic expectation rather than evidence of demonstrated transformation, implementation performance or customer outcomes.
qs: Coming all the way back on that blog post and our core values, this combination of setting up an architectural platform to address those oncoming needs with the myriad data types and volumes, and addressing the use cases that we're seeing in LDI, it all kind of comes together with GENAI to help us conquer that dragon and facilitate that change.

st.t: Legal data: Connected records enable operational transformation
st.an: Saunders supports the need to make legal data usable by distinguishing sensitive, useful and necessary information from large volumes of redundant, obsolete and trivial material. His adoption and retention claims suggest practical demand for AI applied to legal data, but do not establish accuracy, operational transformation or improved legal outcomes.
qs: And that is there is a lot of sensitive, useful and necessary data amongst a massive amount of rot data, right?
This redundant, obsolete, trivial data, which is a huge pool of data to sift through.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of vendors advancing toward agentic workflows and making consequential integration and deployment choices. Relativity’s 2028 cloud requirement concretely illustrates architectural divergence, while its AIR claims are vendor positioning rather than evidence of reliable autonomous delivery; the source does not directly address lawyer supervision or verification.
qs: As you've heard so far, Relativity recently announced that starting in 2028, it's going to require that all new matters be in the cloud, as opposed to on-premises.
Markedly different and brings up, of course, moving from just generative AI capabilities to full up agentic AI workflows, something that we've been on the forefront on with our AIR solution.

kp.k: New matters must move to cloud from 2028
kp.d: Saunders confirms that new Relativity matters will need to use RelativityOne from 2028, while existing Server matters can remain supported for many years. He distinguishes this policy from ending the on-premises product: lengthy legal matters and partners' existing economics justify continued maintenance and security. Customers may choose competing platforms rather than RelativityOne.
qs: The right answer is, leave your existing matters there.
We'll make sure we continue to maintain, secure, and make sure that product is vibrant for you.
But net new matters, three years from now, by the way, will be needed to go into RelativityOne or, humbly speaking, an alternative.

kp.k: Generative AI strengthens the claimed necessity of cloud infrastructure
kp.d: Saunders presents cloud-native performance, capability and security as necessary for generative AI, rather than merely optional benefits. He acknowledges earlier workflow incidents and reliability shortcomings in RelativityOne, saying investment in addressing them preceded the transition announcement. This is the vendor's strategic and technical rationale, not a comparative performance study.
qs: this nature of bringing you to not the desire or optionality for cloud native, but the necessity for it.
It was a really good platform, but not really great at that point in terms of number of incidents customers were having in their workflows, us impacting their business.
the sheer need for cloud native performance capability security

kp.k: Cloud adoption already dominates Relativity's business
kp.d: Saunders reports that RelativityOne represents 75% plus of the business and grew $110 million year over year. He predicts its share should exceed 80% by the end of 2025, explicitly inviting a later check. He also claims investment in the platform exceeds the combined R&D of its top three competitors; these are executive-reported business figures, not independently supplied evidence.
qs: 75% plus of our business is now in RelativityOne.
Should be well over 80% by the end of the year.
RelativityOne grew $110 million
the investment going into that platform is bigger than our top three competitors combined in R&D.

kp.k: Cloud transition disrupts partners' business models
kp.d: Saunders describes mixed partner responses: several strongly support the transformation, while a handful worry about adapting their economics and satisfying owners or private equity. He says Relativity is investing millions of dollars and providing incentives to help partners transition. The mechanism concerns the delivery ecosystem's business models, not just customers' software migration.
qs: there are a handful of partners that are really concerned about it.
how do I transform my business model to address that and appease or serve my owners, my private equity and so on.
We're investing millions of dollars in helping partners make that transition.

kp.k: AI promises workflow transformation rather than human elimination
kp.d: Saunders predicts substantial changes in document review, privilege work, privilege logs and litigation case strategy through AIR. He expects faster work and improved quality and accuracy, but supplies no measured gains. He explicitly retains a critical human role and anticipates changes in law firms, corporate legal and litigation-support teams, and the function and value of legal service providers.
qs: Is it gonna increase the ability to get things done faster? Absolutely.
the importance of the human is still very, very critical
And what is the function and value of a legal service provider, and how does that transform over the course of time, which we think is significant, by the way.

kp.k: Legal data work extends substantially beyond litigation
kp.d: Saunders reports that, in an end-of-January snapshot, roughly 47% of all matters and projects inside RelativityOne were customer-flagged as non-litigation. He identifies FOIA, DSARS, PII, internal disputes, M&A, contracts and data-breach response as examples. He argues that AI can expand the kinds of problems lawyers and support teams address, rather than simply reduce review work; the figure describes platform usage, not the entire legal market.
qs: Roughly 47% of all matters and projects inside RelativityOne, which is flagged by the customer, was non-litigation.
FOIA, DSARS, PII, internal disputes, M&A, contracts, data breach response.
how do we expand the capabilities of law firms, of individual litigators, lawyers, and lit support teams to take on more and different types of work to solve real problems out there?

kp.k: AI development prioritizes governance and agentic workflow augmentation
kp.d: Saunders says Relativity moved data security and governance to the start of customer conversations, including questions about data ownership and Microsoft environments. He describes AI principles, increased R&D, additional teams and scientists as foundations for development. He characterizes AIR as agentic workflow technology using perception and cognition to augment and transform work, rather than a chatbot.
qs: rather than talking about data governance and security later, we actually bring it all the way up front.
we invested a lot more in R&D and created incremental and expansive teams in this area and hired a bunch of scientists
It was literally, before it was cool to say, an agentic AI workflow, literally leveraging the perception and cognition capabilities of AI.

kp.k: Hybrid tools outperform a single-model strategic approach
kp.d: Explicitly presenting his answer as opinion and company perspective, Saunders rejects the idea that generative AI simply replaces machine learning and NLP. He reports running 30 different models across multiple platforms and products against structured data and workloads to assess performance, accuracy, cost and hallucinations. He expects reasoning and research models to enable work agents, while review continues to combine technologies; no comparative results or hallucination rates are supplied.
qs: This is an opinion, Bob, because I think, ask 30 people, you'll probably get 30 different opinions.
We think it is a confluence of tools.
we're running 30 different models across multiple platforms and products
review is going to be transformed.
it's going to continue to look markedly different through a confluence of generative AI, machine learning and other tools.

kp.k: Early AIR adoption supports deployment, not proven outcome gains
kp.d: Saunders characterizes AIR as still at 'day one' while reporting over 100 paying AIR for Review customers, a thousand different workspaces and an active document volume above seven but below 10 million. He reports zero customer churn and over 45 partners and customers engaged in case-strategy work. These figures establish his account of early commercial use, rather than measured accuracy, productivity or workforce effects.
qs: We have over 100 paying customers, a thousand different workspaces
It's above seven, below 10 million documents
It's actually every customer that started has been retained.
I think we have over 45 partners and customers engaged and involved and actively still working case strategy
I think it is absolutely day one.

kp.k: Legal Data Intelligence broadens professional roles and frameworks
kp.d: Saunders describes Legal Data Intelligence as a market-wide initiative co-founded, but not exclusively owned, by Relativity to identify useful legal data amid redundant, obsolete and trivial material. It develops use cases, best-practice archetypes, and definitions of personas and roles beyond e-discovery. He anticipates additional material by its May 2025 first anniversary and describes it as complementary to EDRM, with openness to competitors and other initiatives.
qs: this cannot just be a relativity thing. Like, this is bigger than us.
this redundant, obsolete, trivial data
by this May, we'll be bringing forth some of these additional use cases, and not just the use cases, but the archetypes of how to go about it in a best practice manner.
Definitely use cases, definitely model definitions about personas, roles.
And again, in complement, not in conflict with EDRM.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Phil Saunders predicts that generative AI will transform review, privilege work and litigation strategy, improving quality, accuracy and speed while retaining an important human role.
pts.d: Saunders describes both an ongoing change in users' workflows and an expected further transformation through Relativity's AIR products. He identifies privilege review and privilege logs as particularly demanding work and case strategy as a distinct application beyond discovery. His stated approach is to augment and transform people's work through agentic workflows rather than simply provide a chatbot. He also says AI is transforming regulations, but supplies no concrete regulatory example or mechanism.

pts.k: Saunders expects a combination of generative AI, conventional machine learning and multiple models—not wholesale replacement of earlier techniques—to transform legal review.
pts.d: He explicitly presents this as his and Relativity's perspective. Models should be selected for performance, accuracy, cost and reduction of hallucinations. He says newer deep-reasoning and deep-research models expand what is possible and enable work agents. He anticipates continued capability growth as underlying compute capacity increases.

pts.k: Saunders argues that AI and legal data intelligence can expand legal professionals' work beyond litigation rather than merely reduce existing review work.
pts.d: He connects technology development to growing use cases including FOIA, data-subject access requests, personally identifiable information, internal disputes, M&A, contracts and data-breach response. The Legal Data Intelligence initiative is intended to develop use cases, role definitions and best-practice archetypes across this broader field. His opportunity-expansion claim is not a quantified prediction about employment or an assurance against displacement.

pts.k: Saunders presents generative AI as a driver of cloud-native infrastructure becoming necessary, with consequences for Relativity customers and service-provider business models.
pts.d: He links generative AI and newer reasoning models to requirements for cloud-native performance, security and agility. Relativity's concrete policy is that new matters must move to RelativityOne, or an alternative provider, starting in 2028; existing server matters can remain. He acknowledges that some partners are concerned about adapting their economics and says Relativity is funding transition assistance. This is a vendor platform strategy and supporting infrastructure claim, not a demonstrated universal technical requirement for every legal AI system.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Saunders offers internal adoption and usage figures as evidence that AIR is already being used in live work, but provides no measured quality, accuracy or time-saving results.
pts.d: At the March 2025 interview, he reports over 100 paying AIR for Review customers, about 1,000 active workspaces, more than seven million but fewer than ten million documents, and retention of every customer that started. He also reports over 45 partners and customers engaged in case strategy. These are company-reported adoption indicators, not comparative performance benchmarks or quantified evidence of the predicted productivity gains.

pts.k: The broader claims draw on internal model testing, platform-use data, customer discussions and Saunders' technology-sector experience.
pts.d: For the multi-model claim, Saunders describes testing 30 models with structured data and workloads, without naming tests or reporting scores, error rates or comparative outcomes. For expansion beyond litigation, he cites customer-tagged platform data showing roughly 47% of RelativityOne matters and projects were non-litigation at the end of January 2025; that snapshot demonstrates the reported use mix, not AI-caused growth. For the cloud transition, he reports that over 75% of the business is already in RelativityOne and cites partner feedback. His general predictions also draw on approximately 30 years in technology and extensive customer contact.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Saunders describes transformation as already underway in early 2025 but still at an early stage, with no fixed completion date.
pts.d: He calls AIR's development 'day one,' despite existing adoption, and describes reasoning-model advances over the preceding few months. Further gains depend on ongoing innovation, appropriate combinations of tools, data protection and governance, and willingness to adopt new workflows. Human importance remains explicit, but he does not specify a verification protocol or supervision threshold. The firm policy date is 2028 for new matters; existing server matters will continue to be maintained and secured for years. He separately forecasts RelativityOne's share of business exceeding 80% by the end of 2025, conditional on the data trajectory.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted changes affect law firms, litigators, litigation-support teams, corporate legal departments, legal service providers and Relativity's own vendor business.
pts.d: Lawyers and support teams are expected to perform review and privilege work differently and take on broader legal-data problems. Litigators are a distinct target for case-strategy applications; corporate legal teams are affected through workflow changes and non-litigation uses. Legal service providers face changes in their function, value proposition and cloud-based business economics, including implications for their owners. Relativity is the software vendor enabling and investing in these changes, not itself identified as an alternative legal service provider. Saunders does not quantify job losses, staffing changes, client fee reductions or access-to-justice outcomes.
